newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Mandela eyes Asian investments in Southern Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mandela eyes Asian investments in Southern Africa.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela issued a passionate appeal to Asia on Thursday to see Southern Africa as a lucrative place in which to invest and an anchor trade with South America.
"This region has the potential to be the geographic anchor of new relations among Asian, African and Latin American countries," he said, adding that potential has yet to be exploited.

"Southern Africa today constititues one of the most exciting regions of the world; a region endowed with abundant mineral resources, a market of over 100 million people, great tourist potential, democracy and peace," he said.

Mandela was speaking to business people, scholars and students at the end of a two-day visit to Singapore. He left later on Thursday for Malaysia's capital Kuala Lumpur, the last leg of a four-nation tour of Southeast Asia.
Mandela said South Africa could learn from the region's experience in nation building, saying he was inspired by Southeast Asia's efforts to remove the legacy of inter-ethnic tensions.

"We are driven by a deep desire to rekindle old relationships. We yearn to rebuild what was destroyed. We seek to forge strong multilateral ties among our nations under the new and more favourable conditions of freedom, technological advance and peace," he said.

Mandela urged Asian investors to hurry to South Africa, where economic reforms had opened up "massive mega-projects in mineral processing, petrochemical industries, telecommunications, car manufacturing, tourism, transportation and other infrastructure".
"In all these areas, the contribution of Singaporean and other investors will be critical," he said.

There were "opportunities for large profit margins, the advantage of a sophisticated banking system, the availability of a developed communications network, the freedom to repatriate profits and the advantage of tax holidays in certain designated areas," he said.
Mandela said Southern Africa was working on forging a common destiny as Southeast Asian nations had done.
Such co-operation would eventually spur economic growth and living standards, he said.
"Without ensuring that everyone feels a sense of belonging to the political and economic endeavours of society, there cannot be technological advance, let alone economic growth," he said.
Mandela said democracy would ensure that all who were deprived would be free, and that even the former "colonial oppressors" would be integrated in the new South Africa.
But, he said after his speech; "We have to avoid the minority being the rubberstamp of the majority."
Mandela also called on 14 nations due to meet in Mauritius on Thursday to speed up their bid to form an Indian Ocean Rim economic grouping.
"The idea of the Rim should be pursued with vigour," he said.
"In our interaction with states in Latin America, there is a conviction that the Indian Ocean Rim should be a precursor to similar relations between us and that part of the world."
